newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-SAfrica opens fx doors for private investors.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SAfrica opens fx doors for private investors.

text.p: Individual South Africans will be allowed to invest up to 200,000 ($44,440) overseas from July 1, but officials said they were confident the move would not trigger a fresh run on the rand.

The limit had been widely tipped at around 160,000 rand. The Ministry of Finance said the higher-than-expected allowance was an indication of its commitment to the liberalisation of foreign exhange controls.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said the limit for individual investments was a one-off allowance, but he expected the cap to be increased over time.
Uncertainty about the impact of the July 1 relaxation has dominated trading in South Africa's financial markets recently, with investors nervous the liberalisation could trigger a flight of capital.
The central Reserve Bank moved quickly to soothe these anxieties.
"The chances are good that you will see little, if any, decline in foreign reserves," governor Chris Stals told reporters.

Local liquidity constraints would limit the amount of money which individual South Africans would take offshore, and the Bank had access to 38 billion rand in official reserves and credit lines which it could turn to, he said.

His deputy, James Cross, estimated that between three billion and five billion rand could leave the country following the latest relaxation of capital controls, but this would be roughly matched by inflows.

South Africans will be allowed to hold the 200,000 rand allowance offshore or alternatively in foreign currency deposits with domestic foreign exchange dealers. Residents will be allowed to retain abroad income derived from foreign sources.

At the same time, individuals will be allowed to apply to the exchange control department of the Reserve Bank to invest in fixed property, such as holiday homes and farms in Southern African Development Community member states from July 1.

"I believe that these measures will boost confidence, both domestically and internationally, in the South African economy and lay the foundations for the further liberalisation of the remaining exchange controls in the future," said Manuel.
The rand took the news in its stride in late trading on Wednesday, finishing slightly weaker but off the day's lows at around 4.5050 versus the dollar.

"I think in the short-term you can take it as a positive in the sense that it is not a bad amount and the fact that they are going ahead with foreign exchange control relaxations in general," First National Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Dave Sadler said.
To qualify for the latest relaxation in capital controls, residents will have to sign a declaration of good standing in respect of their South African tax obligations.
The ministry noted that institutional investors had already invested 27.7 billion rand abroad to date under earlier liberalisation measures.
